Both particles are launched with the **same speed**, so every comparison turns on the
angle alone.
**Step 1 — write the maximum height.**
H = v₀² sin²θ/(2g)
With v₀ and g the same for both, H depends only on **sin²θ** ✓
**Step 2 — use the given fact.**
H₁ > H₂
⟹ sin²θ₁ > sin²θ₂
⟹ sin θ₁ > sin θ₂ (both angles acute, so both sines are positive)
⟹ **θ₁ > θ₂** ✓
since sin θ increases throughout 0° to 90°.
**Step 3 — check the time of flight.**
T = 2v₀ sin θ/g
also increases with sin θ, so **T₁ > T₂** as well ✓ This follows from exactly the same
inequality - a higher flight is necessarily a longer one.
**Step 4 — check the horizontal range.**
R = v₀² sin 2θ/g
Here sin 2θ **rises then falls**, peaking at θ = 45° ✓ So a larger θ does **not** mean a
larger range. Take θ₁ = 60° and θ₂ = 30°: H₁ > H₂ as required, yet
sin 120° = sin 60° = 0·866 for both, so **R₁ = R₂** ✗ The claim R₁ > R₂ fails.
**Step 5 — check the total energy.** Both particles have the same mass? Even taking it
so, each is launched with the same speed v₀ from the same level, so each has total energy
½mv₀² throughout ✓ The two are **equal**, so U₁ > U₂ is false ✗
**Why the range behaves differently from the height.** Height depends on the **vertical**
component v₀ sin θ, which grows steadily with θ; range depends on the **product** of the
two components, which is largest when they are equal, at 45° ✓ That is why 30° and 60°
are complementary in range but very different in height.
**A worked comparison.** With v₀ = 20 m s⁻¹ and g = 10 m s⁻²:
θ = 60°: H = 400(0·75)/20 = **15 m**, T = **3·46 s**, R = **34·6 m**
θ = 30°: H = 400(0·25)/20 = **5 m**, T = **2·0 s**, R = **34·6 m**
Height and time of flight rise together; the ranges are identical ✓
**A note on the original.** This comes from a "one or more than one correct" set, in
which the statement about the time of flight is **also** correct, for the reason given in
Step 3 ✓ In the single-answer form used here, the statement about the angles is the one
keyed, and it is the most direct consequence of H₁ > H₂.
∴ angle of projection: θ₁ > θ₂.

Three of these are definitions, true for any motion; one is a special case smuggled in as
a general law.
**Step 1 — check the relation v̄_av = ½[v̄(t₁) + v̄(t₂)].** This averages the **endpoint**
velocities. It is correct only if the velocity changes **linearly** with time, that is,
only under **uniform acceleration** ✓ For motion "in general" - a particle whose
acceleration varies - it is **false** ✗
**A counterexample.** Throw a ball straight up and catch it at the same height. Over the
whole flight v̄(t₁) = +u and v̄(t₂) = −u, so this formula gives v̄_av = **0**. That happens
to be right here, because gravity is uniform. Now take a particle that sits still for
10 s and then jerks to speed v in the last instant: the endpoint average gives v/2, while
the true average displacement rate is nearly **zero** ✗ The formula fails.
**Step 2 — check v̄_av = [r̄(t₂) − r̄(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁).** This is the **definition** of
average velocity: displacement divided by time ✓ True always, for every motion.
**Step 3 — check ā_av = [v̄(t₂) − v̄(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁).** This is the **definition** of
average acceleration: change of velocity divided by time ✓ True always.
**Step 4 — check r̄ = ½(v̄(t₂) − v̄(t₁))(t₂ − t₁).** Dimensionally this is a
velocity x a time, so it could in principle be a length - but it uses the **difference**
of the velocities where a **sum** is needed, and it is written for the position r̄ rather
than for a displacement ✓ Under uniform acceleration the correct statement is
Δr̄ = ½[v̄(t₁) + v̄(t₂)](t₂ − t₁), with a plus sign ✓ As printed, the relation is
incorrect - for a particle moving at constant velocity it gives Δr̄ = 0, though the
particle has plainly moved.
**Step 5 — conclude.** The first relation is the one to tick: it holds only for uniformly
accelerated motion, not in general ✓
**The lesson.** Equations that come from **definitions** - average velocity, average
acceleration - hold universally. Equations that come from **integrating a constant
acceleration** - the familiar v = u + at family, and endpoint averages - hold only while
a is constant ✓ Knowing which is which is what this question tests.
**A note on the original.** In the "one or more than one correct" set it comes from, the
fourth relation is flagged as incorrect too, for the sign reason in Step 4 ✓ In the
single-answer form used here, the first relation is the one keyed.
∴ v̄_av = ½[v̄(t₁) + v̄(t₂)] is the incorrect relation.
